title: How Infections Spread
hook: Germs can't fly to a new host on their own — they hitch rides on coughs, hands, food, water, and insects. Break the ride, and you break the chain of infection.
key_points: Infections are caused by pathogens — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.
Pathogens spread by routes like the air, direct contact, contaminated food or water, and insect bites.
An infection needs a chain: a source, a way out, a route of transmission, and a new host to enter.
Hygiene works by breaking that chain — washing hands and covering coughs remove or block the pathogen.
content_html: Infections happen when a pathogen — a disease-causing bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite — gets into the body and multiplies. But a germ can't simply teleport from one person to the next. It has to travel, and understanding how it travels is the key to stopping it.
extra_html: Spreading an infection takes a chain of events: a source where the pathogen lives, a way out, a route of transmission, and a new host to enter. Those routes are familiar — airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes, direct contact with skin or surfaces, contaminated food and water, or bites from insects like mosquitoes. This is exactly why hygiene matters: washing hands, covering coughs, and cooking food properly each break a link in the chain, removing or blocking the pathogen before it reaches a new host. As Encyclopaedia Britannica's account of infectious disease describes, controlling transmission routes is one of the most powerful tools in public health.

related.title: How Immunity Works
related.hook: Your body fights invaders on two fronts: a fast, general first response that hits anything foreign, and a slower, custom-built defense that learns and remembers each specific enemy.

related.title: Vaccines
related.hook: A vaccine is a training session for your immune system — it learns to beat a dangerous pathogen using a harmless preview, so the real fight is already half-won.

related.title: Are Viruses Alive?
related.hook: A virus is little more than genes in a protein shell — it can't eat, grow, or reproduce on its own, which is why biologists still argue whether it counts as living.

related.title: Why Bird Flu Hid in Cows' Udders
related.hook: Bird flu hit dairy cows in a strange way — striking udders, not lungs. The reason: the receptors H5N1 latches onto are concentrated in mammary tissue, a clue to how it jumps and spreads.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is a common route by which infections spread?

choices.text: Through the air in droplets from a cough or sneeze
Through inherited genes from a parent

flashcards.explanation_html: Many pathogens travel in airborne droplets, but they also spread by touch, contaminated food or water, and insect bites. They aren't inherited.

flashcards.prompt: Why does washing your hands help prevent infection?
flashcards.back_html: It breaks the chain of transmission — physically removing pathogens from your hands before they can reach your mouth, eyes, or another person.

flashcards.prompt: What general name is given to the organisms that cause infectious disease?
flashcards.explanation_html: Pathogens — including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites — are the disease-causing agents. Antibodies and hormones are made by your own body.
